tips.title: Perfect for events, imperfect for background
tips.body: A single completed action takes the **perfect**: *je suis allé*. A description, a repeated habit or the weather takes the **imperfect**: *il faisait beau*, *nous allions*. Most holiday answers need both in the same sentence.

tips.title: Never a future after si
tips.body: *Si* takes the **present** with a future in the other half: *si j'ai le temps, j'irai*. Writing *si j'aurai* is one of the most heavily penalised errors in the paper.

tips.title: Three timeframes earns the top band
tips.body: The best answers move between past, present and future in the same piece. Plan one sentence of each before you start writing, so no timeframe is missing.

tips.title: One holiday or many?
tips.body: The tense follows the question, not the feeling: **one particular holiday** is the perfect (*je suis allé*), while **what you used to do** is the imperfect (*j’allais*). Deciding single or repeated before writing settles the whole paragraph.

why.matters: Holidays are the topic the exam uses to test all three time frames at once: where you used to go, where you normally go, where you will go. The topic exists because the tense chooses itself once the signpost is read, *quand j'étais petit* for the imperfect, *d'habitude* for the present, *l'année prochaine* for the future, and because one past holiday needs two tenses together, the perfect for what happened and the imperfect for what it was like. The top band wants tenses that interact, *si* with the present then a future, *quand* with two futures.

examples.title: Signposts choose the tense
examples.body: Before the verb comes a time word, and the time word has already decided the tense. *Quand j'étais petit* can only be followed by an imperfect; *d'habitude* by a present; *l'année prochaine* by a future; *l'année dernière* by a perfect. Read the signposts first in a listening text and you know what the speaker did rather than does; write them first and the paragraph cannot slip tense halfway through.

visual.alt: A table of holiday signpost phrases with the tense each announces and a French sentence for each, imperfect, present, perfect and future

examples.title: One holiday or many?
examples.body: *Every summer we went to Brittany* is a habit, so imperfect, *nous allions*; *last summer we went to Italy* is one holiday, so perfect, *nous sommes allés*. Inside the story of the one holiday the split runs again: events in the perfect, *nous avons visité Rome*, background in the imperfect, *il faisait chaud, c'était magnifique*. Ask whether it happened once or every time, and the tense follows.

examples.title: Si j'ai assez d'argent, j'irai
examples.body: The top band wants tenses that meet in one sentence. *Si* takes the present and then a future, *si j'ai assez d'argent, j'irai au Canada*, never a future after *si*. *Quand* takes a future in both halves, *quand je serai plus grand, je voyagerai seul*, where English uses a present. The two rules are opposites, and they are the point that separates the grades in this topic.

steps.title: Three times, three tenses
steps.body:
The holidays topic runs across three time frames, and the exam asks about all of them, often in one task: where you **used to** go, where you **normally** go, where you **will** go.

Each frame has its own tense and its own signpost words, and the signposts are the trick. Learn them as a set and the tense chooses itself:

- **Imperfect** for what used to happen: *quand j'étais petit*, *autrefois*, *avant*, *tous les ans* (in the past).
- **Present** for what normally happens: *d'habitude*, *en général*, *normalement*, *chaque été*.
- **Simple future** for plans: *l'année prochaine*, *l'été prochain*, *à l'avenir*, *plus tard*.

The list below has the time words. Read them aloud with the speaker: hearing *prochain* against *dernier* fixes them faster than reading.

visuals.fallback: Les mots du temps: quand j'étais petit(e) — when I was little; autrefois — in the past, formerly; avant — before; tous les ans — every year; chaque été — every summer; d'habitude — usually; en général — generally; normalement — normally; maintenant — now; l'année prochaine — next year; l'été prochain — next summer; à l'avenir — in the future; plus tard — later; l'année dernière — last year; l'été dernier — last summer; il y a deux ans — two years ago

check.prompt: *D'habitude, nous ___ en Espagne.* Which verb form fits the signpost?
check.solution: *D'habitude* means *usually*: a present habit, so *nous allons*.

steps.title: The imperfect: what you used to do
steps.body:
The **imperfect** describes what used to happen and what things were like. You met it last half term; here it carries the childhood holidays.

Stem: the *nous* form of the present with *-ons* removed. Endings: **-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient**. *Aller*: *nous allons* → *all-* → *j'allais*, *nous allions*.

*Quand j'étais petit, nous allions au bord de la mer et nous restions dans un camping.* — When I was little, we used to go to the seaside and stay on a campsite.

Two verbs to have ready: **c'était** (it was) for opinions, and **il y avait** (there was / there were) for what a place had. *C'était génial, il y avait une piscine.*

visuals.alt: The imperfect of aller: j'allais, tu allais, il allait, nous allions, vous alliez, ils allaient

steps.text: *nous allions en Bretagne* — we used to go to Brittany
*nous restions dans un camping* — we used to stay on a campsite
*c'était génial* — it was great
*il y avait une plage* — there was a beach

steps.title: The present: what you normally do
steps.body:
The **present** is for habits, and holidays are a habit for most families: *chaque été, nous partons en Espagne*.

*Aller* is irregular in the present, and it is the verb you will use most, so it has to be automatic: **je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont**.

*Partir* (to leave, to go away) is the other holiday verb: *je pars, nous partons*. *Partir en vacances* is *to go on holiday*.

Habit words go with it: *d'habitude*, *normalement*, *en général*, *tous les ans*, *chaque été*. Notice *tous les ans* works in the present **and** the imperfect; the verb tells you which.

visuals.alt: The present of aller: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont

check.prompt: Which is the present tense *they go*?
check.solution: **Ils vont.** *Allaient* is the imperfect, *iront* the future, *sont allés* the perfect.

steps.title: The simple future: what you will do
steps.body:
Plans take the **simple future**: stem plus **-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont**. For regular verbs the stem is the infinitive (*partir* → *je partirai*, *rester* → *je resterai*, minus the *-e* for *-re* verbs).

The holiday verbs are mostly the irregular ones, so learn the stems:

- *aller* → **ir-**: *j'irai*, *nous irons*
- *être* → **ser-**: *ce sera*, *je serai*
- *avoir* → **aur-**: *j'aurai*
- *faire* → **fer-**: *nous ferons*
- *voir* → **verr-**: *je verrai*
- *pouvoir* → **pourr-**: *je pourrai*

*L'été prochain, j'irai en Italie. Ce sera parfait.*

visuals.alt: The simple future of aller: j'irai, tu iras, il ira, nous irons, vous irez, ils iront
A table of the irregular future stems of the holiday verbs

steps.title: One past holiday: perfect and imperfect together
steps.body:
There are two past tenses, and a holiday story needs both.

**The perfect** is for what happened, one event at a time: *l'année dernière, je suis allé en Italie. Nous avons visité Rome. J'ai nagé dans la mer.* With *être* verbs the participle agrees: a girl writes *je suis allée*.

**The imperfect** is for how things were: *il faisait beau, l'hôtel était génial, il y avait une piscine.*

So *l'année dernière* (one holiday) pulls in the perfect, while *quand j'étais petit* (every holiday) pulls in the imperfect. And inside one story, the events are perfect and the background is imperfect: *il faisait beau quand nous sommes arrivés* — it was sunny when we arrived.

This is the distinction that separates the middle grades from the top ones, and the exam sets it deliberately.

steps.body: The writing task will give you bullets that reach across time. Answer them in order, one signpost and one tense each, and the paragraph structures itself.

steps.title: Going deeper: si, quand, and the tense inside the sentence
steps.body:
The top band wants tenses that **interact**, not three separate paragraphs.

**Si + present, then future.** *Si j'ai assez d'argent, j'irai au Canada.* Never a future after *si*.

**Quand + future, future.** *Quand je serai plus grand, je voyagerai seul.* Both halves future, which English does not do.

**Perfect and imperfect in one sentence.** *Il pleuvait quand nous sommes partis.* Background, then event.

**Opinions in every tense.** *C'était nul* · *c'est agréable* · *ce sera parfait*.

**Agreement with être.** *Je suis allée*, *nous sommes restés*, *elles sont parties*: the participle agrees with the subject. A girl who writes *je suis allé* loses an accuracy mark every time.

And the negative range that examiners list: *ne… jamais* (never), *ne… plus* (no longer). *Je ne pars plus avec mes parents.*

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Signposts choose the tense**: *quand j'étais petit* → imperfect; *d'habitude* → present; *l'année prochaine* → future; *l'année dernière* → perfect.
- **Imperfect**: *nous* stem + *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*. *C'était*, *il y avait*.
- **Present of aller**: *vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont*. *Partir en vacances*.
- **Future stems**: *ir-, ser-, aur-, fer-, verr-, pourr-*.
- **One holiday** is the perfect (*je suis allé(e)*); **every holiday** is the imperfect (*j'allais*). Inside a story, events perfect, background imperfect.
- **Si + present, future**; **quand + future, future**.
- **Agreement** with *être* verbs, and negatives *ne… jamais*, *ne… plus*, for range.

examTechnique.body:
Holidays is the theme the papers use most to test tenses, because it naturally spans time: what you used to do, what you do, what you will do. In the writing paper the bullets are built that way, and the top band needs all three tenses correct and linked. In the speaking picture task and the role play, expect a question in the past and one in the future, and answer in the tense of the question.

The two decisions that decide the grade: perfect or imperfect for a past holiday (one event or a habit; foreground or background), and the future after *quand* against the present after *si*. Signpost every tense change with a time phrase so the examiner sees the range, and check participle agreement after *être* before you hand in.
examinerErrors: Using the imperfect for a single past holiday: *l'année dernière j'allais* instead of *je suis allé(e)*.
Using the present after *quand* for a future plan: *quand je suis grand, je voyagerai*.
Forgetting the *-e* on *allée*, *restée*, *partie* for a female subject.
Answering every bullet in the present, so the range marks are lost even when the content is complete.
Confusing *prochain* (next) with *dernier* (last), which flips the tense.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer moves between the imperfect, the present and the simple future with a signpost for each, uses the perfect for a single past holiday and the imperfect for its background, and links tenses inside sentences with si and quand. Its opinions come in the right tense — c'était, c'est, ce sera — with reasons, its participles agree after être, and it adds range with negatives such as ne… plus.
